title: Our father, our king
hookLine: a litany of requests in the Days of Awe
carry: we have no king but you

cards: A drought in the land of Israel, nearly two thousand years ago. A public fast is called. A great sage stands before the ark and says the long, proper prayers, blessing after blessing.
No rain. Then his student steps up. He doesn't say a long prayer.
He says a few short lines, each beginning with the same two words, words that don't quite fit together. And the Talmud says: the rain came down.

teach.b: The sage was Rabbi Eliezer. The student was Rabbi Akiva. And the two words were avinu malkeinu: our father, our king.
The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, gives his words: our father, our king, we have no king but you. Our father, our king, for your sake, have mercy on us. That was the seed.
Over the centuries, more lines were added, until the prayer became a long litany, in the Ashkenazi rite more than forty lines, each starting the same way.

teach.h: CLOSE AS A FATHER, FAR AS A KING.
teach.b: Our father, our king, inscribe us in the book of good life. Our father, our king, renew for us a good year. Our father, our king, hear our voice.
It's said during the ten Days of Awe, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days. But why those two words together? A father is close.
You can climb into his lap. A king is far. You approach him with care, and he can judge you.
The prayer refuses to choose. God is both: the one who loves you like a parent and the one who holds you to account like a ruler. Some people find the father easier to pray to; some find the king.
The prayer makes you hold both in the same breath, line after line.

teach.h: WE HAVE NO DEEDS; ANSWER US.
teach.b: And then the last line, which many congregations sing slowly, together: our father, our king, be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds; deal with us in righteousness and kindness, and save us.
After all the requests, an admission: we don't have enough to show. Answer us anyway.

how: Avinu Malkeinu is said after the Amidah during the Ten Days of Repentance, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days, usually with the ark open; it is generally omitted on Shabbat, and its last line is often sung together.

games.q: inside Avinu Malkeinu — tap the pairs.
p: we have no deeds; answer us

s: Avinu Malkeinu began as a long litany
it began with a few lines by Rabbi Akiva; lines were added later.
the Talmud says rain fell after Rabbi Akiva's prayer
after Rabbi Eliezer's long prayers didn't bring it.
the last line says we have deeds to show
it says we have no deeds; deal with us in kindness.

games.q: it's a drought. your teacher's long prayers haven't brought rain. you step up. what does Rabbi Akiva say?
o: a few short lines: our father, our king.
games.why: our father, our king, we have no king but you. the Talmud says the rain came down.

practice: If you pray, say avinu malkeinu, or in English, our father, our king, once, very slowly: feel the first word come close, and the second step back.
If prayer isn't yours, think of someone who was both tender and demanding with you, a parent, a coach, a teacher, and hold both sides of them at once.

wordCard.voice: Avinu malkeinu. Our father, our king. Rabbi Akiva's words in a drought, grown into the litany of the Days of Awe.

carryVoice: Your line: we have no king but you. Close and far, in the same breath. Until tomorrow.
